section_1.title: The Problem of Changing Rates
section_1.content: Introduce the fundamental limitation of algebra: it handles constant speeds perfectly, but fails when speed changes constantly. Define the core goal: calculating 'instantaneous' change.
section_1.example: A cheetah accelerating from a standstill to full sprint. We know total distance over time, but how fast is it going at exactly 2.5 seconds?

section_2.title: The Derivative: The Zoom-In Technique
section_2.content: Explain differentiation as the act of zooming in on a curve until it looks like a straight line. Visualizing the 'secant line' transforming into a 'tangent line' as the interval shrinks toward zero.
section_2.example: Visualize a curve of the cheetah's position. Zooming into a single point on the path transforms the curved arc into a straight line, the slope of which is the exact speed.

section_3.title: The Integral: The Summation of Slices
section_3.content: Introduce integration as the inverse operation. Explain it as the process of adding up infinitely many 'infinitesimally thin' rectangles to find the total area under a complex curve.
section_3.example: Calculating the total food consumed by an animal if its eating rate fluctuates throughout the day. By slicing the timeline into thin strips, we sum the area to find the total volume.

section_4.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
section_4.content: Connect differentiation (splitting apart) and integration (putting back together) as two sides of the same coin. This bridge allows us to solve complex physics problems easily.
section_4.example: Showing a graph where the 'area' under a velocity-time graph (integral) perfectly recovers the 'position' (the original function), linking the two concepts visually.

section_5.title: Conclusion: Calculus as the Language of Change
section_5.content: Summarize that calculus is the mathematical tool to quantify change. Whether it's planetary orbits or economic growth, calculus provides the precision to describe our dynamic universe.
section_5.example: A quick visual montage of a rocket launch (physics), a stock market chart (economics), and a heartbeat monitor (biology), all governed by the same derivative and integral principles.
